query: For a multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to simultaneous wear and corrosion at elevated temperature, what single mechanistic hypothesis could explain the accelerated coupled degradation and why it occurs? Specify a controlled comparison capable of distinguishing the proposed explanation, predict the changes in total degradation and the individual wear and corrosion responses relative to a matched baseline, define the relevant boundary conditions, identify supporting evidence, and give a clear falsification criterion.

generation.hypothesis: In multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloys, the fine alternating lamellar architecture promotes preferential localized degradation at phase boundaries under simultaneous high-temperature wear and corrosion. Wear removes protective oxide films at these interfaces, exposing dissimilar phases (soft fcc vs. hard B2) that, due to their different electrochemical potentials, create galvanic couples that accelerate both corrosion and material removal.
generation.material_initial_state: An as-cast multi-phase eutectic high-entropy alloy with a fine lamellar microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard B2 phases.
generation.intervention: Exposure to simultaneous wear (e.g., controlled sliding contact) and corrosion (e.g., immersion in a 3.5 wt.% NaCl solution) at elevated temperatures (around 700°C), compared to control conditions where only corrosion or only wear is applied.
generation.conditions: High temperature conditions that promote accelerated diffusion and oxidation, a corrosive environment (such as NaCl solution), and mechanical wear sufficient to periodically remove protective oxide scales without homogenizing the surface completely. Baseline conditions would involve similar temperature and composition but with isolated application of corrosion or wear.
generation.structural_mediator: The eutectic lamellar structure, specifically the phase boundaries between the soft fcc and hard B2 regions, which become sites of enhanced electrochemical activity and mechanical disruption.
generation.mechanism: Wear-induced removal of protective oxide layers at the lamellar interfaces exposes regions with contrasting electrochemical properties; this fosters localized galvanic interactions that accelerate corrosion. The ensuing corrosion further weakens the phase boundaries, which in turn increases wear particle generation, creating a self-reinforcing cycle of degradation.
generation.predicted_outcome: Under combined wear and corrosion, the alloy will exhibit significantly accelerated total degradation compared to the baseline. Specifically, degradation will be localized at the phase boundaries, with increased corrosion rates and higher wear particle generation due to microstructural delamination. In contrast, under isolated wear or corrosion conditions, the protective oxide films remain more intact, resulting in lower overall degradation rates.
generation.baseline: The same eutectic high-entropy alloy exposed to either isolated wear (in an inert or non-corrosive environment) or isolated corrosion (without mechanical removal of oxide layers) at the same elevated temperature.
generation.boundary: This hypothesis applies to eutectic HEAs with fine lamellar microstructures, under conditions where the temperature is high enough to enhance oxidation/diffusion and where the applied wear is sufficient to remove oxide layers locally but not to completely reform a homogeneous surface layer.
generation.uncertainty: While the mechanism is supported by the noted design strategies and known benefits of lamellar microstructures in eutectic HEAs, quantitative relationships between wear, corrosion rates, and microstructural degradation are uncertain due to potential variations in phase distribution and differences in experimental wear-corrosion conditions.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of multi-phase eutectic HEA samples with identical compositions and microstructures. Subject one set to simultaneous wear (using a controlled sliding tribometer) and corrosion (immersed in 3.5 wt.% NaCl at 700°C) and the second set separately to either isolated wear (in an inert environment) or isolated corrosion (static immersion without mechanical wear) under the same temperature conditions. Compare the spatial distribution of degradation and overall mass loss between the sets.
measurements: Scanning electron microscopy (SEM) imaging to assess the extent and localization of damage along phase boundaries
Electrochemical corrosion rate measurements (e.g., potentiodynamic polarization)
Wear track profiling (e.g., profilometry and surface roughness analysis)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: The hypothesis will be falsified if the combined wear and corrosion condition does not result in significantly higher total degradation, nor show preferential degradation localized at the lamellar interfaces, compared to the isolated wear and isolated corrosion baselines. Uniform degradation across the microstructure or no synergistic increase in degradation rate would refute the proposed mechanism.

cited_evidence.text: High-entropy alloys (HEAs) can have either high strength or high ductility, and a simultaneous achievement of both still constitutes a tough challenge. The inferior castability and compositional segregation of HEAs are also obstacles for their technological applications. To tackle these problems, here we proposed a novel strategy to design HEAs using the eutectic alloy concept, i.e. to achieve a microstructure composed of alternating soft fcc and hard bcc phases. As a manifestation of this concept, an AlCoCrFeNi2.1 (atomic portion) eutectic high-entropy alloy (EHEA) was designed. The as-cast EHEA possessed a fine lamellar fcc/B2 microstructure, and showed an unprecedented combination of high tensile ductility and high fracture strength at room temperature. The excellent mechanical properties could be kept up to 700°C. This new alloy design strategy can be readily adapted to large-scale industrial production of HEAs with simultaneous high fracture strength and high ductility.
